There was the death of Shireen Abu Akleh on 11 May 2022 , and many others even before that . A deeper investigation shows recurring targeted airstrikes , bombs , sniper attacks , shooting and car missile strikes over the past few decades . For instance , in 2002 , Anthony Shadid was shot by an Israeli sniper while reporting for the Boston Globe . In 2018 , Yaser Murtaja , shot in the stomach , was accused of working for Hamas , despite no evidence ever being given . This pattern of silencing journalists stretches back to 1967 . <p> The difference is major in how Israel murdered journalists then versus now . Previously they denied their attacks , hid behind excuses or were vague . Now , they strike while people are watching or broadcasting live on air . Unashamedly now they claim responsibility . Now , there @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ knowing there are zero repercussions for these actions . There is hopelessness in knowing these numbers will grow . Israel is allowed to kill journalists with impunity and the message is clearly -- no one is safe . <p> In Apocalypse Now , the 1979 film directed by Francis Ford Coppolar , creates the story in Vietnam , bringing to life the moral degradation with scenes of savagery , human-worship and one of the most realistic cinematic representations of pure madness captured on screen . When Conrad wrote Heart of Darkness story in 1898 , King Leopold II of Belgium had not even yet carried out his worst atrocities on the Congolese when the heads of men were cut off and hung on village palisades ; women and children 's bodies were assembled in the form of a cross and limbs were cut off for not producing enough rubber . <p> The horror continues , this time through TikTok and Instagram reels broadcast on tiny phone screens . Soon the boats will converge in international waters as a single convoy , sailing under the banner of non-violent defiance . <p> Among the more than 150 participants are three South Africans : Mandla Mandela , grandson of Nelson Mandela ; social leader Zaheera Soomar , based in the United Arab Emirates ; and Cape Town occupational therapist Fatima Hendricks . It warned that unlawful attacks in international waters or detention of participants " will lead to accountability " . <p> The risks are real : Israel has previously intercepted flotillas in international waters , drawing global condemnation . The answer , when it comes , will decide not only Gaza 's fate but the credibility of international law itself , and the meaning of " never again " .

The war in Gaza has been the subject of so much focus , in fact , that the war in Ukraine has largely faded in the public consciousness , while those untold thousands of children and innocent civilians affected by often far worse conflicts in places like Sudan , Myanmar , Syria , Haiti , Ethiopia and the DRC seem to merit barely a second thought . <p> Those same " peace advocates " who have vilified every action Israel has taken from the morning of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as a half-hearted condemnation a couple of months ago when just a few kilometres away from the Israeli border , Syrian Islamists massacred hundreds of innocent Druze - in a manner that directly mirrored Hamas ' massacre of Israelis on October 7th , as it so happens . <p> This is n't a question of " whataboutism " -- though I suppose one could accuse it of that - but of moral consistency , hypocrisy , and a selective outrage that is reserved entirely for the Jewish State . It 's a bizarre hysteria that can turn smart , perfectly reasonable people into brain-dead zombies who see red at the merest mention of Israel . <p> Examples of this are too numerous to mention , but they can be found in every corner of anti-Israel activism . @@129592015 <h> Zille 's attitude is one of colonial denial hiding behind the mask of efficiency <p> Helen Zille 's recent appearance on Newsroom Africa drew attention for her casual dismissal of Israel 's genocidal violence in Palestine . This was not just a passing remark . It revealed an attitude that goes beyond one politician . <p> It captured a way of thinking that prizes order and efficiency while pushing aside questions of justice . This way of thinking has a long history . It comes from the colonial playbook , and today it sits comfortably in neoliberal politics . <p> Colonial powers justified their rule through denial . They portrayed indigenous peoples as inferior and depicted conquest as the progress of civilisation , development and law . Beneath this rhetoric of progress , there were forced removals , violent massacres and , most starkly , the genocide committed in Namibia in the early 1900s against the Herero and Nama peoples . <p> This mindset reframed atrocities as accidents . It turned destruction into something regrettable but inevitable . Responsibility was shifted onto the colonised . The same logic operates @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and destroyed universities are not recognised as evidence of genocide . They are written off as collateral damage . This denial strips Palestinians of their humanity and makes their suffering invisible . <p> In today 's politics , denial is often dressed up in the language of efficiency . Competence and delivery are presented as neutral virtues . But in practice , they protect privilege . They keep us from facing inequality . They reduce justice to order and cast transformation as disruption . <p> The Democratic Alliance ( DA ) has made this its brand . It tells voters that managerial skill and technical competence are the highest political virtues . Within this frame , restitution and redress fall away . Zille 's dismissal of genocide flows directly from this outlook . It shows how the language of efficiency can be used to excuse denial . <p> She has now declared her candidacy for Johannesburg mayor in next year 's local elections . The city faces crises such as inequality , exclusion , widespread corruption and failing services , calling for bold reforms . But Zille offers efficiency -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The city is in crisis . It has been badly mismanaged for years . People are exhausted by endless promises while traffic lights fail , potholes grow , water outages continue and power failures become a daily occurrence . <p> It is also true that Cape Town , governed by the DA , runs more efficiently and has less corruption than Johannesburg . A city can not be rebuilt on moral bankruptcy . What South Africa needs is a new form of politics -- one that combines efficiency with ethical seriousness . We need leaders who can run cities competently , without @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ present , that option is not on the ballot paper . <p> The Palestinian struggle can not be understood in isolation . Its people are subjected to forced removals , restrictions on movement and denial of political rights . We know these realities . We recall the pass laws , Bantustans and racial segregation . <p> To disregard these parallels is to deny the shared history of colonised peoples . It breaks the chain of solidarity that links struggles for dignity across continents . It treats Palestine as an exception when it is part of a wider pattern of oppression . <p> The language of efficiency is rarely neutral . It secures privilege by narrowing politics to administration . It reassures the powerful that nothing fundamental will change . <p> Applied to Palestine , this perspective diminishes genocide to a matter of governance . Mass death is recast as a security issue . Structural violence is regarded as a technical issue . Neutrality becomes complicity when violence is left unnamed . <p> A politics of restitution begins with recognition of harm . It accepts responsibility and affirms that justice requires @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tackling the legacies of apartheid : land inequality , economic exclusion and segregated living spaces . It requires recognising Palestinians as fully human . <p> Efficiency and accountability matter , but they only have value when connected to justice . Efficiency must serve redistribution . Anti-corruption efforts must bolster fairness . Without this broader vision , efficiency is an empty slogan . <p> Our transition shows what happens when efficiency is separated from justice . @@129710622 <p> An SA president has to be both a president and a prime minister , because the country 's modified parliamentary system merges the roles of head of government and head of state into a single office . <p> As prime minister Cyril Ramaphosa is the head of the executive branch of government , chosen by and accountable to parliament and required to maintain the " confidence " of the legislature to remain in office . He sits at the apex of a centralised administrative system , controlling cabinet appointments , influencing budget allocations and wielding authority within the governing coalition . He also has to win elections on his party 's ticket . <p> Simultaneously he is the head of state , a role that in most parliamentary systems is held by a separate , often ceremonial , figure such as a monarch or a figurehead president . As head of state he has to rise above daily partisan politics to represent and speak for the entire nation . <p> These two roles sit uneasily together . The partisan and inherently divisive nature of a prime minister 's job @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ president . A successful leader must navigate these tensions , but no postapartheid president has fully succeeded in this task . <p> Nelson Mandela was a president but not a prime minister , excelling at the symbolic , unifying presidential role but showing little interest in the administrative machinery of state , delegating those prime ministerial duties to his deputy , Thabo Mbeki . <p> Mbeki was the opposite : a prime minister but not a president . He expertly managed the state apparatus and policy process , but his political style was divisive and factional , and he failed to provide the unifying presidential leadership the country needed . <p> Jacob Zuma used his prime ministerial power to appoint cabinet members as a tool for patronage , disrupting the state for personal and factional goals . His presidential leadership was limited , appealing mainly to his provincial base and traditional leaders rather than the whole nation . <p> Ramaphosa has done his best to combine these roles with some dignity , rebuilding state institutions undermined by his predecessors and keeping his party together while also looking to provide unifying @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> However , the tensions in SA 's political system become extreme when overlaid by a second challenge : a president has to lead overseas but also address crises at home . @@129784177 <p> Almost six months since it was discovered and exposed that a number of South African journalists had been on a paid junket to Israel , the office of the Press Ombud has made an important finding against the publications . <p> In an interesting turn of events that hold huge lessons for media platforms in relation to Israel 's genocide in Gaza and the need to be mindful of not being played by the Zionist regime 's lobbyists , the industry owes a debt of gratitude to sharp-eyed consumers . <p> In this case , as in previous matters related to an abuse of the Press Code , the complainant has been a well known media-analyst and social justice activist , Hassen Lorgat . <p> The three publications whose journalists were sponsored by a Zionist-affiliated South African Jewish Board of Deputies ( SAJBD ) were the Sunday Times , the Citizen and BizNews . <p> --&gt; <p> As BizNews is not a member of the Press Council and not subject to its jurisdiction , it was excluded from the ruling . <p> The core of the complaint by Lorgat @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their journalists were sponsored by the SAJBD . <p> He argued that by withholding and concealing this crucial fact , both newspapers were not only in breach of the Press Code , but also in violation of fundamental media ethics especially under the prevailing circumstances of SAJBD 's ally Israel 's ghastly genocide in Gaza . <p> My reading of the events as it unfolded is that it was common knowledge that the Zionist regime 's abysmal public relations was at an all time low in need of boosting , yet to fall for a fully paid PR junket was inexcusable . <p> --&gt; <p> Neither of the two newspaper 's editors could argue - though they did n't dare to - that they were ignorant or unaware of the enormous negative impact on Israel 's standing in global public opinion . <p> Inspite of it , to agree to allow senior journalists on the junket , and to add the proverbial " insult to injury " , to conspire to conceal that it was a trip sponsored by a known ally of Israel , was both unprofessional and unethical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Press Code which reads : <p> The media shall : <p> --&gt; <p> 2.1 not allow commercial , political , personal or other non-professional considerations to influence reporting , and <p> avoid conflicts of interest as well as practices that could lead readers to doubt the media 's independence and professionalism ; <p> 2.2 not accept any benefit which may influence coverage ; <p> 2.3 indicate clearly when an outside organisation has contributed to the cost of newsgathering ; and <p> As pointed out by Franz Kruger , the Deputy Press Ombud , of specific relevance is clause 2.3 , which requires members to disclose any sponsorship . <p> It is clear that the newspapers were in breach of clause 2.3 when the reports were first published . <p> " Public trust in journalism is undermined when it is open to manipulation by vested interests or can be seen to be open to manipulation . Reporting simply can not be for sale and sponsorship is rarely , if ever , disinterested , " wrote Kruger . <p> He further found the " failure to disclose the SAJBD sponsorship by the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ relationship of trust the media must maintain with audiences . @@129821632 <p> 1 . This application has generated a lot of noise . Geopolitics , antisemitism , and genocide are all raised on multiple occasions . There are accusations of bad faith . <p> 2 . Much of the noise drowns out what this application is actually about . <p> 3 . At its core , the merits of the application turn on a straightforward review of public power . <p> 4 . To assist this Court in assessing the true issues in this matter , the applicant files four volumes of written submissions . <p> --&gt; <p> 4.1 . This volume , Volume One , concerns the merits of the review . <p> 4.2 . Volume Two concerns the issues raised on the pleadings that are irrelevant to the merits . <p> 4.3 . Volume Three concerns costs . <p> 4.4 . Volume Four provides a detailed chronology . <p> --&gt; <p> ( ii ) The nature of this application <p> 5 . On 22 June 2024 , the Council of the University of Cape Town ( UCT or the university ) took a decision to pass two resolutions . <p> 6 . The first resolution includes a clause rejecting " the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance 's conflation of critique of Zionism and Israel 's policies as antisemitism in favour of the Jerusalem Declaration 's dynamic understanding of what constitutes antisemitism " .1 <p> 7 . In terms of the second resolution , " no UCT academic may enter into relations , or continue relations with , any research group and/or network whose author affiliations are with the Israeli Defence Force , and/or the broader Israeli military establishment " .2 <p> 8 . This is a review of Council 's decision to pass these two resolutions.3 <p> 9 . The review rests on six grounds , any of which suffices to set aside Council 's decision . <p> 10 . First , the Chair of Council and members of Council 's Executive Committee ( Exco ) knew of a risk that if passed the resolutions would result in UCT losing three substantial donations valued at hundreds of millions of rands . Members of Exco failed to disclose this risk before Council took its decision , despite being asked repeatedly by Council members about the potential implications of passing the resolutions.4 <p> 11 . Second , Council failed to consider several relevant and material factors before taking its decision . These factors include financial implications , a risk report from 2019 about similar resolutions , and three legal opinions on Council 's powers to pass resolutions limiting academic freedom . <p> 12 . Third , the decision is irrational . The first resolution seeks to reject the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance ( IHRA ) definition of antisemitism because it supposedly conflates antisemitism with criticism of Israel . But the IHRA definition makes it clear that " criticism of Israel similar to that levelled against any other country can not be regarded as antisemitic " .5 The second resolution is too broad , too narrow , and too vague to achieve any legitimate purpose.6 <p> 13 . Fourth , Council acted unlawfully . It had no authority to pass the two resolutions under the Higher Education Act 101 of 1997 ( HEA ) , its 2010 policy on public statements , and the Regulations for Reporting by Public Higher Education Institutions.7 These instruments mean that Council could only pass the resolutions if they were reasonable . But the resolutions are not reasonable . They impose disproportionate limits on the constitutional right to freedom of expression , which includes academic freedom . <p> 14 . Fifth , Council failed to consider the views of affected persons and stakeholders . <p> Council was obliged to consider stakeholder views before taking its decision , as a matter of rationality and in terms of its own Risk Management Policy of June 2020 . <p> 15 . Sixth , there is a reasonable apprehension of bias . Several Council members , including the Chair of Council , have through their views and public statements on the subject matter of the resolutions created a reasonable apprehension that Council was biased when it decided to pass the resolutions . <p> 16 . These heads of argument set out each ground of review . They then deal with remedy . <p> ( Reporting Regulations ) . <p> B. GROUND ONE : NON-DISCLOSURE <p> 17 . Council exercised public power , in terms of section 27(1) of the HEA , when it passed the two resolutions.8 <p> 18 . Council , consequently , was bound to exercise its powers according to the principle of legality.9 The principle of legality requires Council to act lawfully , rationally , and in good faith.10 <p> 19 . Council did not do so on the facts of this case , because there was a failure by certain members of Council to disclose a known risk of losing three donations should Council pass the two resolutions . <p> ( i ) The facts of this case <p> 20 . The Chair of Council and Exco members knew that if Council passed the two resolutions , then UCT risked losing at least three donations.11 <p> 21 . First , a donation of R200 million from the Donald Gordon Foundation ( the DGF ) towards UCT 's Neuroscience Institute . <p> 21.1 . In September and November 2023 , the Chair of Council signed two ( substantively similar ) donor agreements with the DGF.12 <p> 21.2 . These agreements included a clause obliging UCT to adopt " a zero-tolerance attitude to antisemitism , defined by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance " .13 UCT drafted the final wording of this clause.14 <p> 21.3 . On 19 April 2024 , Senate passed the two resolutions that Council ultimately adopted on 22 June 2024 . These included the first resolution , rejecting the IHRA definition.15 <p> 21.4 . The then Vice-Chancellor has admitted that Senate 's first resolution breached the terms of the donor agreement with the DGF.16 <p> 21.5 . On 26 April 2024 , the director of the Neuroscience Institute , the beneficiary of the donor agreement , emailed the Chair to inform him that Senate 's resolutions were a " major concern " for the DGF . He explained that the DGF is considering cancellation of the donor agreement , " which would be disastrous for the Neuroscience Institute , and for UCT more broadly " .17 <p> 21.6 . On 30 April 2024 , the DGF wrote to the Chair informing him that UCT had breached the donor agreement through Senate 's rejection of the IHRA definition.18 <p> 21.7 . On 3 May 2024 , the DGF emailed the Chair repeating that it considered UCT in breach.19 <p> 21.8 . Also on 3 May 2024 , the DGF met with the Chair . The DGF informed him that the DGF intended to cancel the donor agreement if Council passed the resolutions.20 The Chair does not deny that he was so informed ; he alleges that he " does not have any recollection of being warned at this meeting " that the DGF would cancel if Council passes the resolutions.21 Mr Appelbaum of the DGF has confirmed on oath that the Chair was informed of the DGF 's intention to cancel should Council pass the resolutions.22 <p> 21.9 . On 13 May 2024 , the then Vice-Chancellor confirmed the Chair 's understanding that the DGF was concerned about the resolutions , and recorded the Chair 's commitment to the DGF " to facilitating constructive engagements on the Israel- Palestine issue " .23 <p> 21.10 . On 23 May 2024 , the then Vice-Chancellor informed Exco members at a meeting that the DGF had placed UCT in breach of the donor agreement . Exco was informed of the DGF 's letter placing UCT in breach.24 The DGF 's concerns " were fully discussed " at this meeting.25 Exco understood " the DGF to have made a legitimate threat to cancel the donor agreement " .26 Exco then discussed " manipulation by funders that had a pro-Israel stance " .27 <p> 21.11 . On 22 June 2024 , the Chair and Exco members thus knew of at least a risk and " some threat " that the DGF would cancel its R200 million donation to the Neuroscience Institute if Council passed the resolutions.28 <p> 21.12 . The then Vice-Chancellor admitted as much , after the fact , at Council 's meeting of 27 July 2024 . At this meeting , he admitted that the DGF letter of 30 April 2024 , placing UCT in breach , had created a risk that UCT would lose R200 million if Council passed the resolutions.29 <p> 22.1 . Throughout 2023 and 2024 , the DGF and UCT discussed a donation valued at hundreds of millions of rands either to acquire the UCT Private Academic Hospital31 or to fund the establishment of an entirely new hospital.32 <p> 22.2 . The proposed donation was significant , and the project had positive potential . <p> By the middle of 2024 , there was every indication that the donation would proceed.33 Two working groups had been formed . These groups met multiple times , and visited a similar project at the University of the Witwatersrand.34 <p> 22.3 . As with the donor agreement with the DGF , on 26 April 2024 , the director of the Neuroscience Institute emailed the Chair to inform him that the DGF was considering withdrawing from the private hospital donation because of Senate 's resolutions.35 <p> 22.4 . On 23 May 2024 , during the Exco meeting , the DGF 's concerns " were fully <p> 22.5 . On 22 June 2024 , the Chair and Exco thus knew of the risk of losing the DGF private hospital donation should Council pass the two resolutions . <p> 22.6 . The Chair admits that he understood that the DGF was considering making a sizable donation.37 He admits that the DGF had committed to donating or had indicated that it would donate the private hospital ( though the monetary value of that donation had not been finalised ) .38 He admits that because of Council passing the resolutions , UCT lost the opportunity to continue discussions with the DGF about the donation , and as a result lost the opportunity of a possible donation.39 <p> 23 . Third , a shared grant agreement with the Michael and Susan Dell Foundation ( the Dell Foundation ) valued at R6 755 000 for the continued support of selected UCT students . <p> 23.1 . On 6 November 2023 , the Dell Foundation and UCT ( represented by the then Vice-Chancellor ) entered an agreement by which the Dell Foundation would donate funds to support UCT students . <p> 23.2 . Between 18 March 2024 and 10 April 2024 , the Dell Foundation wrote to UCT to express its concerns about various developments on campus , including the defacing of a Holocaust memorial , Israeli Apartheid Week , and the polarisation on campus around certain issues.40 <p> 23.3 . On 21 April 2024 , after Senate passed its resolutions and UCT failed to respond to the Dell Foundation 's concerns about student wellbeing and safety , the Dell Foundation decided to cancel its direct funding partnership with UCT.41 <p> 23.4 . UCT 's Executive Director for Development and Alumni ( DAD ) at the time described this decision as " momentous " .42 <p> 23.5 . On 2 May 2024 , the Dell Foundation met with the then Vice-Chancellor to arrange for the terms of the Dell Foundation 's exit from UCT . At this meeting , the Dell Foundation " strongly reinforced that if UCT 's Council were to pass the motions on or after 22 June 2024 , it would further negatively impact the relationship and ability for the Foundation to reconsider its position and scholarship awards in the future " .43 The then Vice-Chancellor does not deny <p> that the Dell Foundation informed him of this ; he alleges only that he has " no recollection " of the Dell Foundation conveying this position to him.44 <p> 23.6 . On 23 May 2024 , the then Vice-Chancellor informed Exco members that the Dell Foundation was " suspending " funding because of Senate 's resolutions.45 The Chair explains that " the concerns of the donors were fully discussed " at this meeting.46 <p> 23.7 . On 22 June 2024 , based on its correspondence and the Exco meeting , the Chair and Exco members knew of ( at least ) the risk of the Dell Foundation withdrawing funding because of the resolutions.47 On the Chair 's version , he and Exco members knew on 22 June 2024 that the Dell Foundation was waiting to see the outcome of Council 's meeting before deciding on its future with UCT.48 <p> 23.8 . On 27 July 2024 , after the fact , the then Vice-Chancellor admitted in a Council meeting that on 22 June 2024 the relationship between UCT and the Dell Foundation had been at risk due to the resolutions.49 <p> 24 . The Chair plainly knew of the risk of losing the three donations.50 He had signed the donor agreements with the DGF himself and was present at the Exco meeting of 23 May 2024 . During Council 's meeting of 22 June 2024 , he lamented the " day that we are held sort of hostage or to ransom because , you know , we are going to lose funding " . He even said that if losing funding is a concern , " then we will need to be upfront about it " .51 <p> 25 . Despite knowing of the risks of losing the three donations , the Chair and Exco failed to disclose the known extent of that loss or possible loss.52 None of the correspondence with the DGF or the Dell Foundation was placed before Council.53 The transcript of the Council meeting reveals that no Exco member raised the concerns of the DGF or the Dell Foundation.54 <p> 26 . Council members , other than the Chair and Exco , did not otherwise know of these risks.55 The Chair admits that not all Council members knew of the risks.56 <p> ( ii ) The legal consequences <p> 27 . There are three legal consequences to the failure by the Chair and Exco to disclose known risks relating to the three donations : Council failed to consider relevant information , the Chair and Exco breached their fiduciary duties , and the Chair and Exco demonstrated bias and bad faith . <p> ( a ) Failure to consider relevant considerations <p> 28 . If Council , by ignoring relevant material , adopts a means that bears no rational link to a legitimate purpose , then Council has acted irrationally.57 <p> 29 . Council can only take decisions in the best interests of the university.58 <p> 30 . A real risk of losing substantial donations to the direct benefit of students and staff is relevant to whether a decision -- like passing the resolutions -- is in the best interests of the university . <p> 30.1 . The risks of losing the three donations directly impacted on students and staff . <p> The Dell Foundation funded 209 students directly.59 UCT 's Neuroscience Institute was the beneficiary of the DGF donor agreement , the withdrawal of which was " disastrous " for the Institute.60 <p> 30.2 . The donations were of substantial amounts and of significant value to the university . By any measure , R200 million , funding for over 200 students , and a hospital are substantial donations to a university . Withdrawal of the donations was described by UCT staff as " disastrous " and " momentous " .61 <p> 30.3 . Council members asked after the risks of losing funding . A Council member , in the deliberation proceeding Council 's decision , asked after the " potential implications " of Council passing the resolutions.62 Another said that " it behoves us as fiduciaries of this university to think about what the implications would be for our university if we were to adopt this particular resolution " .63 Another stressed that they could not vote to adopt the resolutions until somebody explained " what the implications of that for the university are " .64 <p> 30.4 . At the beginning of the Council meeting , the then Vice-Chancellor presented to Council that UCT was " privileged " to have received the R200 million donation from the DGF.65 Council was thus told of the existence of the donor agreement , but not of the fact that UCT had been placed in breach of that agreement ( and that the then Vice-Chancellor considered the Senate resolutions to have put UCT in breach ) .66 <p> 31 . The Chair contends that the risks of losing the three donations were too remote to warrant disclosure.67 However , the risks were far from remote . <p> 31.1 . The DGF had sent a formal letter and an email alerting UCT to its breach ; the then Vice-Chancellor admits that Senate 's resolutions , which served before Council , placed UCT in breach.68 <p> 31.2 . The Dell Foundation had already cancelled its donor agreement.69 <p> 31.3 . Both donors warned the Chair or the then Vice-Chancellor that a decision by Council to pass the resolutions would further jeopardise their relations with UCT.70 <p> 31.4 . The Chair and the then Vice-Chancellor were in " anxious " talks to try to address the DGF 's concerns.71 The very fact that the Chair and the then Vice-Chancellor had ongoing engagements with the DGF to " resolve their concerns " with the Senate Resolutions suggests that there was a real risk of losing their donations.72 <p> 31.5 . The Exco understood " the DGF to have made a legitimate threat to cancel the donor agreement " , 73 and that the Dell Foundation ( at least ) had " suspended " funding due to the Senate resolutions.74 <p> 31.6 . A Council member , at the meeting of 22 June 2024 , asked about the potential implications of passing the resolutions . The risks did not need " certainty " , only potential , to warrant disclosure.75 <p> 31.7 . The Chair 's allegation that the risks " were not yet ripe " for disclosure thus does not withstand scrutiny.76 <p> 32 . Council could not act in the best interests of the university without considering the impacts of its resolutions on students and staff . Failure to consider the risks regarding the donations , as a means to take a decision , bears no rational link to taking a decision in the best interests of the university . Without obtaining and considering information regarding the impact , amounts , and risks of losing the donations , Council could not assess the financial harm of its resolutions and its impact on students and staff , which are among the central considerations of acting in the university 's best interests.77 <p> 33 . Council did nothing to mitigate the irrationality of its process . The non-disclosure of the risks in the process leading up to Council 's decision meant that the decision was made without any reliable sense of its impact on students , staff , and the university community . If a central feature of acting in the university 's best interest is to mitigate adverse impacts of decisions on students and staff , then a process that failed even to consider those adverse impacts is inevitably coloured with irrationality.78 <p> 34 . Accordingly , the failure to disclose the risks of losing the donations rendered Council 's decision irrational . <p> ( b ) Breach of fiduciary duty <p> 35 . Council members owe fiduciary duties to UCT.79 These fiduciary duties are imposed by statute . Section 27 of the HEA requires Council to " govern " the university and that its members participate in deliberations in the best interests of the university . Item 4 of the Manual to the Reporting Regulations imposes various governance responsibilities on Council , including to act in the best interests of the university and to " act as the focal point for and custodian of governance in the institution " . Section 12 of UCT 's Institutional Statute lists the various functions of Council , all of which form part of its general duty to govern the university.80 Section 16(1A) repeats the statutory injunction that " members of council must participate in the deliberations of the council in the best interests of the University " .81 <p> 36 . Acting in the university 's best interests requires disclosing known material information <p> to Council before it takes a decision . <p> 36.1 . The Constitutional Court held in Gelyke Kanse : " No sensibly functioning higher education institution can afford to be without senior persons in its governance structures , who are both skilled in finance and knowledgeable about the institution 's own needs , risks and opportunities . " 82 <p> 36.2 . Recently , Kriegler J affirmed this duty in the context of a report to the Council of Stellenbosch University : " A chairperson should always disclose significant circumstances in the interests of transparency and good governance . " 83 <p> 37 . The fiduciary duty borne by Council members to disclose known relevant information is analogous to the duty borne by directors of companies . <p> 37.1 . The Companies Act 71 of 2008 obliges directors to communicate to the board at the earliest practicable opportunity any material information that comes to the director 's attention.84 <p> 37.2 . At common law , the duty to communicate known relevant information to a board of directors is an integral part of the duties of loyalty , good faith and the avoidance of a conflict of interest.85 <p> 37.3 . Directors breach this duty when they keep cards close to their chest , causing fellow directors to " not know what they did not know " .86 <p> 38 . Accordingly , by failing to disclose the known risks of losing the three donations , the Chair and Exco breached their fiduciary duties to the university . Since these duties are imposed by statutes , that renders Council 's decision unlawful.87 <p> ( c ) Bias and bad faith <p> 39 . Decision-makers exercising public power must be impartial : nemo iudex in sua causa.88 <p> 40 . By failing to disclose the known risks of losing the donations , the Chair and Exco failed to act impartially . These risks were within their knowledge and were adverse to passing the resolutions . But they failed to disclose the risks , despite being asked , manifesting bias in favour of the resolutions.89 <p> 42 . The Chair and Exco did not act transparently and honestly , contrary to the requirement of good faith.91 Had the Chair and Exco been transparent and honest , they would have disclosed the known risks of losing the donations , certainly after being asked after the " potential implications " of the two resolutions . Instead , by keeping the risks of losing the donations to themselves , they hoped to get away with a " surreptitious connivance " .92 <p> 43 . Accordingly , the Chair and Exco were biased and acted in bad faith . This bias and bad <p> faith taints Council 's resolutions . <p> C. GROUND TWO : FAILURE TO CONSIDER RELEVANT FACTS <p> 44 . As explained above , if Council , by ignoring relevant material , adopts a means that bears no rational link to serving the best interests of the university , then Council has acted irrationally contrary to the principle of legality.93 <p> 45 . In addition to the real risk of losing three donations , Council failed to consider at least eight relevant considerations.94 The failure to consider each factor , and certainly the cumulative failure to consider all this information , decouples the means adopted by Council to take its decision from any legitimate purpose , and taints the entire process with irrationality . <p> ( i ) First relevant consideration : financial consequences <p> 46 . Council passed the resolutions without any prior assessment of the potential costs of the resolutions to UCT.95 <p> 47 . These financial implications extend beyond the donations by the DGF and the Dell Foundation . The Vice-Chancellor explained on 19 October 2024 that other donors have withdrawn from UCT and the resolutions have impacted prospective donors and future funding.96 The University Audit and Risk Committee on 7 December 2024 explained that donors have removed UCT from their wills and major donors have cancelled long-term commitments.97 There are also material risks that UCT loses funding , whether grants or donations , from the United States and Germany.98 <p> 48 . Council failed to consider any of these consequences or their possibility before taking its decision . As one Council member puts it , it " is likely that the consequences of Council 's decision will not be fully known any time soon " .99 <p> 49 . The financial consequences of a decision by Council are relevant to whether a decision is in the best interests of a university , certainly when Council members ask after and acknowledge that there may be potential financial consequences.100 <p> 50 . Financial consequences may be outweighed by other considerations , for example moral imperatives.101 But to decide whether financial consequences are outweighed by other factors , one needs to know of and consider those financial consequences . In this case , Council did not first consider the financial consequences and then attribute a certain weight to them in a balancing exercise.102 Council failed to consider the financial consequences at all.103 <p> 51 . Council provides no proper reason for its failure to consider financial consequences . <p> The Chair suggests that a failure to consider financial consequences was justified because of " a risk " that UCT " could " contribute to human rights violations and international crimes in Gaza.104 However , there was no evidence before Council of this risk . Council , when it took its decision , had not conducted an audit of the number of academics who had relations with groups linked to the Israel Defense Forces ( the IDF ) .105 Even if this risk existed , it still needed to be and could have been assessed against the financial consequences of the resolutions . There was no urgent , pressing reason to pass the resolutions without assessing financial repercussions . <p> 52 . In these circumstances , Council , without considering any financial consequences , could not have acted in the best interests of the university . An important part of the university 's interests is financial . Without assessing the impact of a decision on those finances , Council does not know if overall its decision is in the best interests of the university . Council 's decision , taken without consideration of financial consequences , was thus irrational . <p> ( ii ) Second to fourth relevant considerations : the March 2019 resolution <p> 53 . This is not the first time UCT has passed resolutions concerning Israel . <p> 54 . On 15 March 2019 , Senate adopted a resolution : " UCT will not enter into any formal relationships with Israeli academic institutions operating in the Occupied Palestinian Territories as well as other Israeli academic institutions enabling gross human rights violations in the Occupied Palestinian Territories . " The March 2019 resolution included a proviso : " Individual academics , students , and departments are free to engage in academic pursuits with anyone as they wish guided by their own conscience . " 106 <p> 55 . Before Senate adopted the March 2019 resolution : <p> 55.1 . On 31 August 2017 , the Academic Freedom Committee ( AFC ) held a special meeting to hear presentations from the Palestinian Solidarity Forum ( PSF ) and the South African Union of Jewish Students ( SAUJS ) regarding the wording of a proposed resolution concerning Israel.107 <p> 55.2 . On 25 April 2018 , Senate 's Executive Committee met with the AFC to discuss its proposals regarding the resolution.108 <p> 55.3 . On 23 November 2018 , Senate voted to reject proposed resolutions by the AFC and the PSF . It did so after considering a statement by the university 's executive that boycotts risk academic freedom , do not advance solutions to conflicts , and have chilling effects on debates.109 <p> 56 . After Senate adopted the resolution : <p> 56.1 . On 30 March 2019 , Council refused to adopt Senate 's resolution . It required clarification on several issues , a sustainability impact assessment report , and a consultation process with the university community . It sent the matter back to Senate.110 <p> 56.2 . On 17 May 2019 , Council obtained an opinion by Adv Michael Bishop . The opinion advised that Council could not lawfully pass a resolution like the March 2019 resolution.111 <p> 56.3 . On 10 May 2019 , Senate decided to adopt a consultation process facilitated by the university 's executive.112 <p> 56.4 . Between 6 and 21 June 2019 , UCT community members could respond to a survey with their views regarding the March 2019 resolution.113 <p> 56.5 . On 22 June 2019 , Council resolved to require Senate and the executive to present to Council their recommendations regarding the March 2019 resolution considering the public consultation process and an impact assessment report.114 <p> 56.6 . On 19 August 2019 , ikapadata ( Pty ) Limited compiled a report summarising the responses to the survey concerning the March 2019 resolution . It found that 65% of respondents objected to the resolution.115 <p> 56.7 . On 12 September 2019 , the AFC obtained a legal opinion from Professor John Dugard SC on whether Israel commits human rights violations , whether Israeli universities operating in the Occupied Palestinian Territories are lawful under <p> international law or South African law , whether universities in Israel enable gross violation of human rights , and if so whether UCT would have any legal duties in relation to those universities.116 <p> 56.8 . Sometime after 12 September 2019 , Council obtained another opinion from Adv Bishop to respond to the Dugard opinion . This supplementary opinion concluded that the Dugard opinion did not change the advice of the first Bishop opinion : Council could not adopt the March 2019 resolution.117 <p> 56.9 . On 22 November 2019 , Senate resolved to rescind the March 2019 resolution . <p> Senate did so for various reasons . The resolution went beyond symbolic gesture , could apply to every Israeli institution , and there was no reason to " single out Israel for condemnation while UCT continued to have relationships with academic institutions in other countries that were engaged in human rights violations " .118 <p> 56.10 . Around January 2020 , UCT 's executive received a report on the sustainability impact of the March 2019 resolution.119 This Impact Assessment Report strongly urged UCT against passing a resolution like the March 2019 resolution . It cited risks of litigation , losing funding from the US and Germany , losing donations , staff cutbacks , declines in research output , and polarisation . The report predicted " catastrophic " losses to UCT of between R660 million and R330 million.120 It warned of a " very high " risk of " potentially upwards of 50 black students per annum " losing funding.121 <p> 56.11 . The report concluded that UCT can not " approve a resolution such as the recent Senate resolution forming the topic of this investigation , and at the same time claim to be acting in the best interest of the institution -- this would simply not be true " .122 <p> 56.12 . The report records that its findings " could yield potentially useful information for the University for future use " .123 <p> 57 . Council failed to consider any of these materials when passing the resolutions impugned in this application.124 It did not consider the minutes from the Senate meetings of 2018 and 2019 , the Impact Assessment Report , and the three legal opinions . After the institution of these proceedings , one Council member was " surprised by the facts concerning the background to the 2019 resolutions " .125 <p> 58 . These materials were relevant to Council 's decision . The Chair alleges that differences between the March 2019 resolutions and the two impugned resolutions meant that Council did not need to consider these materials.126 In particular , the March 2019 resolution targeted Israeli institutions , while the second resolution on 22 June 2024 prohibits collaborations with academics affiliated with the IDF and the broader Israeli military establishment.127 <p> 59 . However , these differences do not render irrelevant -- <p> 59.1. the concerns raised in Senate in 2018 and 2019 , after consulting the AFC , about limiting academic freedom , singling out Israel , not achieving solutions to the conflicts involving Israel , and chilling debate ; 128 <p> 59.2. the advice given in the two opinions by Adv Bishop about Council 's legal powers to limit academic freedom and to pass resolutions limiting academic collaboration ; <p> 59.3. the advice given in the Dugard opinion about whether Israel is in breach of international law and guilty of gross human rights violations , including by academic institutions in Israel ; 129 and <p> 59.4. the " catastrophic " risks highlighted by the Impact Assessment Report , particularly the " pro-Israel " Trump administration 's possible response to a resolution targeting Israel , the position of the German government , and the risk of donors withdrawing from UCT.130 <p> 60 . The substantial similarities between the resolutions mean Council ought to have considered the materials surrounding the March 2019 resolution -- especially the Impact Assessment Report , which detailed the adverse consequences for students and staff.131 Its failure to do so renders its decision irrational . <p> 61 . For similar reasons , Council 's failure to consider the minutes of the Senate meetings leading up to Senate 's passing its resolutions on 19 April 2024 renders Council 's decision irrational . <p> 62 . Before its meeting of 19 April 2024 , when it passed its two resolutions , Senate met five times.132 <p> 63 . Although there were significant shortcomings in the Senate deliberations themselves , 133 these five meetings nevertheless included pertinent discussions concerning polarisation on campus , academic freedom , meaningful engagement on global crises , current collaborations between UCT and Israeli academics , the need to refrain from making statements on behalf of the entire university , litigation risks , and the risks of financial repercussions ( as highlighted by the Impact Assessment Report ) .134 Senate also debated the IHRA definition.135 One Council member regrets not considering these discussions by saying " deliberations before Senate about the definition would have also assisted Council " .136 <p> 64 . The Chair concedes that these minutes were relevant to Council 's decision -- twice . <p> 64.1 . First , on 19 September 2024 , Council wrote that " the record which has been filed contains all information relevant to the impugned decisions or proceedings " .137 The record filed included minutes from Senate 's five meetings . But Council did not consider these minutes.138 <p> 64.2 . Second , in his answering affidavit , the Chair contends that the second resolution should be interpreted " in the context of the proposer 's motivation and the discussions that informed its amendment and adoption by the Senate and Council " .139 So , on his own version , Council lacked the materials required to interpret the second resolution . <p> ( iii ) Fifth relevant consideration : Council 's 2010 policy <p> 65 . When Council passes a policy , then that is UCT 's official position.140 <p> 66 . When Council took the decision to pass the two resolutions , it failed to consider Council 's 2010 policy on making public statements.141 <p> 67 . The 2010 policy is the university 's official position on making public statements . It was passed by Council and contains guidelines Council intended for Council to consider before adopting a public statement.142 Accordingly , Council ignored factors that itconsidered relevant to its decision . No explanation is given for this failure to consider these factors.143 This is irrational . <p> 68 . Council failed to consider at least two guidelines in the 2010 policy . <p> 69 . First , whether Council can make its statement with " clear " authority.144 The Chair appears to consider himself an expert on the IDF , Gaza , and antisemitism ; he thinks that the situation in Gaza and the status of the IHRA definition are " obvious and manifest " .145 But he is no such expert , 146 no one else on Council is or claims to be , and the situation in Gaza and the status of the IHRA definition are subject to good faith debate by reasonable people.147 The point is that Council did not consider these factors , and its " clear " authority to pronounce on Gaza , the IDF , and antisemitism , before taking its decision . Council did not even consult with an expert before passing its resolutions.148 <p> 70 . Second , whether Council 's position " will command widespread ( though not necessarily unanimous ) support within the UCT community " .149 The Chair alleges that Council considered this factor by considering the fact that Senate had passed the two resolutions.150 However , Senate represents only one part of the UCT community , 151 and one can hardly imagine a more controversial topic than the Israel-Hamas conflict.152 The Chair admitted as much , during the meeting of 22 June 2024 , when he said the resolutions are " clearly a divisive issue " .153 Council thus did not consider whether the resolutions would find the support of the thousands of students , staff and alumni who are not members of Senate . Council did so in 2019 , but the Chair provides no explanation for why Council did not do so before 22 June 2024.154 <p> 71 . Accordingly , Council acted irrationally by failing to consider its 2010 public statement policy and the guidelines contained in it . <p> ( iv ) Sixth relevant consideration : the AFC <p> 72 . Unlike in 2019,155 Council failed to consider the views of the AFC before passing the two resolutions.156 Council members who sit on the AFC failed to convey the views of the AFC to Council.157 Council received no document from the AFC regarding the justifiability of the resolutions.158 <p> 73 . The AFC 's views on the resolutions were materially relevant . First , Mr Arendse concedes as much by invoking the AFC 's views to defend the resolution in this application.159 Second , the AFC 's terms of reference make clear that the AFC exists " to advise Senate and Council on any aspect of academic freedom , including University autonomy " .160 Third , Council can not decide something in the best interests of the university without understanding the impact it has on academic freedom -- according to its own academics . <p> ( v ) Seventh relevant consideration : the consequences of breach <p> 74 . Council did not consider or determine the consequences of breaching the impugned resolutions.161 <p> 75 . During the meeting of 22 June 2024 , a Council member asked after the consequences of breach . No-one answered his question , or responded to his objection that passing the resolutions without considering the consequences for breach would be " the height of irrationality " .162 <p> 76 . The Chair concedes that the two resolutions need to be reasonable.163 We explain in Part E below why they are not . <p> 77 . The point here is more fundamental . If Council 's decision needed to be reasonable , then the consequences of breaching the resolutions were materially relevant . Reasonableness or proportionality can only be assessed considering the nature and extent of a limitation on any rights . That nature and extent is determined by the consequences of breaching the resolutions.164 If there are no consequences to breach , then the limitation is not as severe as , for example , disciplinary sanction for breach . <p> 78 . By failing to consider the consequences of breaching the resolutions , Council failed to consider whether its resolutions were reasonable . It failed to consider whether it complied with its duty to govern , which as it accepts entails a duty to act reasonably . <p> This is irrational : Council can not act in the best interests of the university without knowing whether its decision is reasonable . <p> ( vi ) Eighth relevant consideration : the definitions <p> 79 . The IHRA definition and the Jerusalem Declaration do not appear in the rule 53 record.165 <p> 80 . The Chair alleges that Council members were familiar with the two definitions . <p> However , at least one Council member has stated that he had not encountered the definitions before the meeting of 22 June 2024.166 <p> 81 . Council did not consider academic commentary regarding the IHRA definition and the Jerusalem Declaration.167 It did not consider the views of IHRA , including academics who work at or assist IHRA.168 It did not consider the views of academics who signed the Jerusalem Declaration , including the applicant 's views.169 It had no relevant materials before it pertaining to the IHRA definition or Jerusalem Declaration . One member of Council , having now seen the materials attached to the Chair 's affidavit , explains that these materials would have assisted Council in taking its decision.170 <p> 82 . The failure to consider the definitions and commentary on those definitions is plainly irrational , given that Council was considering whether to reject the IHRA definition and adopt the Jerusalem Declaration . <p> 83 . The Chair alleges that materials regarding IHRA were publicly available.171 He admits that Council members should have prepared for their meeting by considering these materials relating to the IHRA definition.172 However , he never alleges that he or any member of Council actually considered the materials he attaches to his answering affidavit prior to the meeting of 22 June 2024.173 He can not do so . There is no evidence that he or Council members considered these materials , or any other materials relating to the IHRA definition , before passing the resolutions . <p> ( vii ) Conclusion on relevant considerations <p> 84 . What would a rational process leading up to the two resolutions look like ? <p> 85 . The answer is found at leading universities around the world . Since 7 October 2023 , scores of universities have grappled with antisemitism and how to respond to the situation in Gaza . Had Council bothered to look , it may have discovered that these leading universities adopted robust public consultation processes , often led by experts from various backgrounds , before coming to resolutions.174 <p> 86 . In contradistinction , Council passed the two resolutions considering only two documents : the actual resolutions . It did not consider the impact of the resolutions on staff , students , and the broader UCT community ( as it did in 2019 ) . A barely quorate Council rushed the resolutions through right at the end of its last meeting before a new Council was constituted.175 This process renders Council 's decision irrational . <p> D. GROUND THREE : SUBSTANTIVE IRRATIONALITY <p> 87 . If the two resolutions bear no link to a legitimate purpose , then they are irrational.176 We demonstrate below that neither resolution substantively bears a rational link to a legitimate purpose . <p> ( i ) The first resolution <p> 88 . The first resolution includes a clause rejecting " the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance 's conflation of critique of Zionism and Israel 's policies as antisemitism in favour of the Jerusalem Declaration 's dynamic understanding of what constitutes antisemitism " .177 <p> 89 . On its own terms , the purpose of the first resolution is to reject the IHRA definition 's <p> 90 . However , the IHRA definition does not conflate antisemitism with criticism of Israel . <p> It says : " criticism of Israel similar to that levelled against any other country can not be regarded as antisemitic " .179 It provides examples , which include Israel , that " could , taking into account the overall context " , be antisemitic.180 This is no categorical conflation of antisemitism with criticism of Israel.181 <p> 91 . The Chair appears to acknowledge this . He provides another rationale in his affidavit . <p> He contends that the first resolution rejects the IHRA definition because the IHRA definition has been weaponised to stifle legitimate speech . Thus , the purpose of the first resolution is to protect academic freedom from the abuse of the IHRA definition.182 <p> 92 . There are several difficulties with this rationale . <p> 93 . First , if the rationale behind the first resolution was to address or prevent the abuse of the IHRA definition , then Council adopted an irrational process . <p> 93.1 . Council had no evidence before it of supposed " weaponisation " of the IHRA <p> definition . <p> 93.2 . Council also had no evidence before it of the efficacy of the IHRA definition , and how numerous reputable bodies use the definition responsibly.183 <p> 93.3 . UCT had not previously adopted the IHRA definition . The definition could not therefore have been abused before then to silence academics at UCT.184 The Chair admits : " I am unable to comment on the extent to which the IHRA definition has restricted academic speech in South Africa . " 185 <p> 93.4 . The materials the Chair attaches to his affidavit , which concern the use of the IHRA definition at other universities , are ex post facto justifications , which were not before Council , were not considered by Council members , 186 and which can not be used to justify Council 's decision.187 <p> 93.5 . Council thus could not rationally take a decision regarding the abuse of the IHRA definition , because there was no basis before it for a conclusion that the IHRA definition is prone to abuse or has even been abused ( certainly at UCT ) .188 <p> 94 . Second , the Chair provides opinion evidence in contending that the IHRA definition has been abused or weaponised , 189 with the necessary implication that the Jerusalem Declaration has not been . The Chair is not an expert on the IHRA definition or the Jerusalem Declaration.190 He provides this Court with no appreciable help on the issue of the IHRA definition , not only because the Chair is no expert but also because actual experts ( including the applicant and the Advisor to IHRA ) dispute the Chair 's opinion.191 The Chair 's opinion evidence is thus inadmissible , 192 but also unsustainable . <p> 95 . Third , if the rationale behind the first resolution is to protect academic freedom and the weaponisation of antisemitism , then it arbitrarily excludes the other definitions of antisemitism that can be abused to silence criticism of Israel . The Chair alleges : if a definition is open to " irresponsible use " , then it is not fit for purpose.193 The Jerusalem Declaration , which the first resolution endorses , has been criticised by the Palestinian Solidarity Campaign and Middle East experts of being weaponised to silence Palestinians.194 Indeed , any definition of antisemitism could be abused in this way.195 There was thus no reason to single out the IHRA definition ; the resolution is arbitrary.196 <p> 96 . Fourth , the first resolution arbitrarily selects one set of academics ' freedom over another 's . <p> 96.1 . Mr Arendse does not contend that any use of the IHRA definition is abusive , only that the definition can be and has been abused.197 In fact , he suggests that UCT academics may legitimately use the IHRA definition in their research.198 <p> 96.2 . The IHRA definition then can be used legitimately and illegitimately -- on his version . <p> 96.3 . By rejecting the definition categorically , Council 's first resolution thus prohibits legitimate and illegitimate uses of the IHRA definition . <p> 96.4 . By prohibiting illegitimate uses of the IHRA definition , the resolution aims to protect the academic freedom of those academics who may be victims of the abuses of the IHRA definition . At the same time , by prohibiting legitimate uses of the IHRA definition , the resolution limits the academic freedom of academics who legitimately use the IHRA definition.199 For instance , the applicant 's research team uses the IHRA definition for collecting data on online hate speech.200 <p> 96.5 . The resolution thus limits the freedom of one set of academics in favour of another set of academics . <p> 96.6 . The Chair never gives a reason for protecting the academic freedom of those who might be silenced by abuses of the IHRA definition over those who use the IHRA definition legitimately . This is arbitrary.201 <p> 96.7 . Both sets of academics are entitled to academic freedom ; their rights are equal in value and significance ; there is no hierarchy between them.202 It may be that conflicting individual academic 's rights may at times need to be balanced if they conflict with each other . But there must be a reason for requiring one academic 's rights to yield to another's.203 That reason can not only be " promoting academic freedom " , because both academics enjoy the right to academic freedom . <p> 96.8 . Stated differently , if the rationale behind the first resolution is only to prevent the abuse of the IHRA definition in the name of academic freedom , then the only rational means of achieving that rationale is to prohibit the abuse of that definition ( and in fact any definition ) -- not the definition itself.204 Any attempt to prohibit legitimate uses of the definition invariably limits academic freedom , and without more that academic freedom is of the same value and significance as the academic freedom enjoyed by those who may be silenced by illegitimate uses of the IHRA definition . <p> 97 . Accordingly , the first resolution is irrational and arbitrary . It does not link to a legitimate purpose . <p> ( ii ) The second resolution <p> 98 . The second resolution reads : " no UCT academic may enter into relations , or continue relations with , any research group and/or network whose author affiliations are with the Israeli Defence Force , and/or the broader Israeli military establishment . " 205 <p> 99 . The Chair alleges that the rationale behind the second resolution is to prevent any association of UCT 's research with allegations of possible gross violations of human rights and breaches of international criminal justice and international humanitarian law.206 <p> 100 . The resolution does not seek to prevent violations of human rights and international crimes , whether by the IDF or any other entity.207 The resolution concerns UCT 's reputation . It seeks to protect UCT from associations with allegations of possible unlawful conduct.208 <p> 101 . The second resolution bears no rational link to this purpose . <p> 102 . First , if its rationale is to protect UCT 's reputation , then Council adopted an irrational <p> process before passing the second resolution . <p> 102.1 . Council did not consider the possible adverse impacts the resolution may have on its reputation . <p> 102.2 . For instance , the 2019 Impact Assessment Report considers the risks of UCT being excluded from academic networks for limiting academic freedom by passing a resolution inhibiting relations with Israeli academic institutions.209 Council failed to consider these risks . <p> 102.3 . Council , moreover , did not consider the position of any other university before passing the second resolution.210 In the event , no other leading university in the world has passed a resolution like the second resolution that limits individual academic relations.211 <p> 102.4 . Council thus acted irrationally . It failed to consider how other universities and academic networks would view the second resolution when the purpose of the resolution was to protect UCT 's reputation among those universities and academics.212 <p> 102.5 . The proof of the pudding is in the eating . After passing the resolution , an international academic network of which UCT is a part , and which planned to host a conference at UCT , described the second resolution as " unpleasant " , " vague and unclear -- and thus unpredictable " , and contrary to its basic principles.213 <p> 103 . Second , the resolution is so underinclusive that it is arbitrary and without a link to its purpose . <p> 103.1 . The second resolution targets allegations of possible human rights violations and international legal breaches only by the IDF and the broader Israeli military establishment . <p> 103.2 . However , the resolution does not account for how UCT could attract associations with allegations of possible human rights violations and breaches of international law by any other person or entity . For instance , the second resolution fails to address any UCT associations with allegations of possible rights violations or international wrongs committed by Hamas , Russia , China , the US , or Iran.214 <p> 103.3 . If the rationale behind the resolution is to protect UCT 's reputation , then there is no reason why only allegations of possible wrongs involving the IDF fall within the ambit of the resolution . UCT 's reputation stands to be affected by all allegations of possible gross human rights violations and international legal breaches . The resolution is thus arbitrary and bears no link to its purpose . <p> 103.4 . The second resolution is also underinclusive insofar as breaches of human rights and international law by Israel are concerned . The second resolution prohibits relations with " any research group and/or network whose author affiliations are with the Israeli Defence Force " ( emphasis added ) . So , a UCT academic could receive funding directly from the IDF or the Israeli government , even for research linked to the IDF 's conduct Gaza , insofar as there is no relation with a " group " or " network " with an " author affiliation " to the IDF.215 <p> 103.5 . Additionally , the resolution applies only when an " author affiliation " links to the IDF or the broader military establishment . But Israeli academics can have a university as their institutional " home " , but research for the IDF . Thus , the second resolution permits research with those university academics even though they may research ( exclusively ) for the IDF and possibly be complicit in unlawful conduct.216 <p> 103.6 . This is irrational . If part of the purpose of the second resolution is to prevent UCT 's association with unlawful conduct by the IDF and the Israeli government , then for no reason the second resolution excludes obvious examples of such association -- like direct funding . It fails to prevent UCT 's association with possible unlawful conduct committed by the IDF and Israel . <p> 104 . Third , the policy is so overinclusive that it is arbitrary and without a link to its purpose . <p> 104.1 . Just because a UCT academic enters a " relation " with a research group or network whose author affiliations are with the IDF or " the broader Israeli military establishment " does not mean that the academic commits or is complicit in an international crime or a gross violation of human rights . <p> 104.2 . The research could be entirely neutral to international legal violations . For example , if the applicant co-authored a paper on religious observance in the IDF with a rabbi affiliated with the IDF , then he has committed no international crime or gross violation of human rights.217 <p> 104.3 . The research could even be against international legal violations . The Chair admits that a UCT academic could not author a paper on atrocities committed by the IDF , or on how the IDF could comply with international law , with someone whose author affiliation is the IDF or the broader military establishment.218 <p> 104.4 . The research could also be remote from Israel and the IDF . The prohibition in the second resolution applies to collaborations " whether directly or indirectly through intermediary institutions " .219 The second resolution thus , for example , prohibits collaboration with a research group if that group is part of a network of research groups and any one of those groups in that network includes someone who is affiliated with the IDF.220 This is immense overbreadth . <p> 104.5 . Additionally , to attract scrutiny under the second resolution , an academic needs to attract any allegation of possible unlawful conduct.221 The resolution casts a very wide net . Academics are singled out for such scrutiny if there is an allegation of unlawful conduct , not actual unlawful conduct . The allegations can be made by any person , not only other UCT academics . The allegations need not identify actual unlawful conduct , but only possible unlawful conduct.222 <p> 105 . Fourth , the second resolution is impermissibly vague , so much so that it can not link to its purpose . <p> 105.1 . There is no reasonable clarity on the meaning of " broader military establishment " .223 Council members have acknowledged that they do not understand what this term means.224 The Chair says : " ' broader militaryestablishment ' encompasses institutions that are formally and presently part of Israel 's military establishment " .225 This is a circular explanation . <p> 105.2 . The Chair explains that the second prohibition would proscribe relations with a unit in the IDF that engages in or funds research -- even though no-one in that unit is a researcher whose author affiliation is the IDF.226 Though not reasonably clear -- and this is the problem -- the Chair reads the second resolution as prohibiting relations with any group or network " under the auspices of the IDF " .227 " Author affiliation " plays no limiting role.228 <p> 105.3 . The second resolution prohibits collaborations " whether directly or indirectly through intermediary institutions " .229 As explained above , there is thus no reasonable clarity on which groups or networks are caught by the second resolution . As the applicant explains : " I work with a diverse array of people and networks . Those people and networks , in turn , also work with a diverse array of people and networks . Whether those people or networks happen to have relations with persons whose author affiliations are the IDF is simply impossible for me to ascertain . " 230 <p> 105.4 . The Chair inconsistently refers to the second resolution prohibiting relations with academics who are formally affiliated , 231 active and formally affiliated , 232 active or formally affiliated , 233 or just active , 234 in relation to the IDF.235 The word " active " has no reasonably clear meaning , which is why Senate rejected amending the resolution to include " active " .236 <p> 105.5 . Thus , the resolution provides no reasonable clarity to UCT academics . Without that reasonable clarity , it can not rationally further the purpose of protecting UCT 's reputation and falls foul of the rule of law.237 <p> ( iii ) Conclusion on rationality <p> 106 . If the point of the first resolution is to protect academic freedom , then Council acted irrationally by not considering evidence regarding the abuse ( and use ) of IHRA , failing to prohibit the abuse of other definitions of antisemitism ( including the Jerusalem Declaration ) , and arbitrarily preferring one academic 's freedom over another 's . <p> 107 . If the point of the second resolution is to protect UCT 's reputation , then Council acted irrationally by not considering the adverse effects the resolution might have on its reputation , and by adopting a vague resolution that is over- and underinclusive . <p> E. GROUND FOUR : UNREASONABLENESS <p> 108 . The Chair and Council correctly admit that Council resolutions must be proportionate to a legitimate purpose . Resolutions must be reasonable and justifiable.238 <p> 109 . Council passes resolutions under section 27(1) of the HEA . The section obliges ( " must " ) Council to " govern " . " Govern " must mean " reasonably govern " . As Council governs , it is inevitable that Council may on occasion limit constitutional rights . Its resolutions may impact on academic freedom , 239 peaceful and unarmed assemblies , 240 unfair discrimination , 241 freedom of thought , belief , and opinion , 242 and dignity.243 Interpreting " govern " to promote the spirit , purport , and objects of the Bill of Rights -- as this Court must -- entails requiring Council , when its governing limits constitutional rights , to do so reasonably and justifiably.244 Otherwise , Council would violate constitutional rights.245 <p> 110 . Assessing whether Council governs reasonably when limiting constitutional rights entails considering the factors set out in section 36(1) of the Constitution . Council 's resolutions must be reasonable , considering the nature of the right limited , the purpose of the limitation , the extent of the limitation , the relationship between the limitation and the purpose , and the availability of less restrictive means . A court weighing up these factors must arrive at a global judgment on the proportionality of the limitation.246 <p> 111 . The onus is on Council to demonstrate that its resolutions are a reasonable limitation of constitutional rights.247 <p> 112 . Council did not govern reasonably when it passed the two resolutions . <p> ( i ) The first resolution <p> 113 . The first resolution , by rejecting the IHRA definition , limits the right in section 16(1) of the Constitution to freedom of expression , including academic freedom.248 <p> 113.1 . The content and scope of the right to freedom of expression are broad.249 <p> 113.2 . The effect of the first resolution is to prohibit academics from using the IHRA definition legitimately in their research.250 <p> 113.3 . The Chair denies any limitation and contends that individual academics can continue to use the definition in their research.251 <p> 113.4 . This allegation is without merit . The first resolution implies that any academic using the IHRA definition will be scrutinised for or suspected of " weaponisation " and conflating antisemitism and criticism of Israel.252 The first resolution states the university 's " position " on the definition of antisemitism.253 It at least creates a chilling effect , 254 deterring academics from using a definition that the " official position " of the university rejects.255 This limits their academic freedom . <p> 114 . This limitation is unreasonable and unjustifiable . <p> ( a ) The purposes of the limitation <p> 115 . The purpose of the first resolution is to reject the IHRA definition 's supposed conflation of antisemitism with criticism of Israel . This purpose is illegitimate . As explained above , the IHRA definition does not conflate antisemitism with criticism of Israel . <p> 116 . The other supposed purpose of the first resolution is to protect the academic freedom of those academics who may be accused of antisemitism and otherwise silenced by abuses of the IHRA definition.256 As explained above , protecting the academic freedom of those academics is important , but it is no more important than protecting the academic freedom of those academics who use the IHRA definition legitimately . This purpose behind the first resolution thus adds little , if anything , to the proportionality analysis . <p> ( b ) The nature of the right limited <p> 117 . The right limited by the first resolution -- the right to freedom of expression -- lies at the heart of a democracy.257 The right recognises the moral agency of individuals and <p> facilitates the search for truth.258 It is one of a " web of mutually supporting rights " , closely tied to the rights to freedom of belief ( section 15 ) , dignity ( section 10 ) , freedom of association ( section 18 ) , political rights ( section 19 ) , and the right to assembly ( section 17 ) .259 These rights -- <p> " operating together , protect the rights of people not only individually to form and express opinions , but to establish associations and groups of like-minded people to foster and propagate their views . They confirm the importance , both for a democracy and the individuals who comprise it , of being able to form and express opinions -- particularly controversial or unpopular views , or those that inconvenience the powerful . " 260 <p> 118 . The right to freedom of expression extends to expression that shocks , disturbs , and offends.261 " We have to put up with views we do n't like . " 262 The right demands tolerance and open-mindedness ; a commitment not to approbate every view , but to the " public airing of disagreements and the refusal to silence unpopular views " .263 As the Supreme Court of Appeal has held regarding section 16 : <p> " The fact that particular expression may be hurtful of people 's feelings , or wounding , distasteful , politically inflammatory or downright offensive , does not exclude it from protection . Public debate is noisy and there are many areas of dispute in our society that can provoke powerful emotions . The bounds of constitutional protection are only overstepped when the speech involves propaganda for war ; the incitement of imminent violence ; or the advocacy of hatred that is based on race , ethnicity , gender or religion , and that constitutes incitement to cause harm . . . . Many may deplore certain statements , but that does not deprive them of constitutional protection . " 264 <p> 119 . It is no coincidence that the Constitution guarantees the right to freedom of expression : <p> " Having regard to our recent past of thought control , censorship and enforced conformity to governmental theories , freedom of expression - the free and open exchange of ideas - is no less important than it is in the United States of America . It could actually be contended with much force that the public interest in the open market-place of ideas is all the more important to us in this country because our democracy is not yet firmly established and must feel its way . Therefore we should be particularly astute to outlaw any form of thought control , however respectably dressed . " 265 <p> 120 . Academic freedom , as part of the right to freedom of expression , has a particular nature and importance . <p> 121 . The academy is responsible for the production of society 's most reliable knowledge ; and it facilitates the production of knowledge as an end.266 This knowledge is generated by experts who are free to enquire , research , and teach.267 Academic freedom exists to protect this production of knowledge and pursuit of truth , both on a personal268 and institutional basis.269 A former Chief Justice of South Africa thus described academic freedom as " sacred " , and consisting of the freedom to decide " what to teach , whom to teach , how to teach and who should teach it " .270 <p> ( c ) The nature and extent of the limitation <p> 122 . The extent of the limitation is severe.271 The first resolution deters UCT academics from using the IHRA definition in their research .
