Use of the IHRA definition will invariably invite censure and suspicion , because the university 's official position is that the definition conflates antisemitism with criticism of Israel , that it is weaponised to silence legitimate criticism , and that anyone who uses the definition is " pro-Israel " .272 <p> 123 . Chilling effects have a particularly pernicious effect in academia . " Where suspicion fills the air and holds scholars in line for fear of their jobs , there can be no exercise of the free intellect . Supineness and dogmatism take the place of inquiry " .273 " Scholarship can not flourish in an atmosphere of suspicion and distrust " .274 <p> 124 . Thus , in striking down an Arkansas law that prohibited teaching " the theory or doctrine that mankind ascended or descended from a lower order of animals " , the US Supreme Court reiterated that academic freedom " does not tolerate laws that cast a pall of orthodoxy over the classroom " .275 <p> 125 . The first resolution casts that pall of orthodoxy . It says to academics and students : IHRA 's definition can not be used , and the Jerusalem Declaration can be . It stifles debate and use of a widely accepted and defended definition of antisemitism.276 Instead of allowing academics to explore and use the definition freely , the first resolution communicates that the university has taken a side in , and decided on , an ongoing academic debate . <p> ( d ) The relationship between the limitation and its purpose <p> 126 . As explained above , the limitation is not narrowly tailored to its purpose.277 If the purpose is to prevent abuse of definitions of antisemitism , then ( a ) there is no need to reject the IHRA definition per se , but only its abuses and ( b ) the first resolution fails to reject or prohibit the abuse of other definitions of antisemitism.278 The first resolution thus fails to be reasonably capable of achieving its purpose.279 <p> ( e ) Less restrictive means <p> 127 . There was simply no need for Council to pass the first resolution.280 The most obvious less restrictive means is not to reject or adopt any definition of antisemitism . That way , the university could not abuse or weaponise that definition to silence legitimate criticism of Israel ; the university will not limit those academics who use the definition legitimately from conducting their research ; and the university can address alleged instances of abuse between academics if they arise.281 Everyone wins . <p> 128 . If UCT nonetheless wanted to affirm its commitment to protecting academic freedom , then Council could have passed a resolution condemning all stifling of academic freedom , and all abuses of concepts , including antisemitism , meant to silence academics . It did not need to reject the IHRA definition and adopt the Jerusalem Declaration . <p> ( f ) Conclusion on reasonableness of the first resolution <p> 129 . Rejecting the IHRA definition , and adopting the Jerusalem Declaration instead , is an unreasonable measure to protect academics from abuses of that definition . It stifles academic debate unnecessarily and with little link to protecting academic freedom . <p> 130 . Perhaps , for these reasons , over 345 universities around the world have endorsed the IHRA definition , including the top research university in the world.282 <p> ( ii ) The second resolution <p> 131 . The Chair admits that the second resolution limits the right to freedom of expression , including academic freedom.283 This is correct . The resolution precludes academics from collaborating and researching with other academics . <p> 132 . The limitation imposed by the second resolution is unreasonable . <p> 133 . The purpose behind the resolution is to protect UCT 's reputation . Council seeks to avoid associations with allegations of possible unlawful conduct.284 In principle , this is a legitimate purpose . Council may take steps to protect and advance UCT 's reputation " among the leading research universities in the world " .285 <p> 134 . We have discussed the nature and importance of the right to freedom of expression , including academic freedom , above . <p> 135 . The extent of the limitation imposed by the second resolution is severe . We have explained how the resolution is overbroad and vague . Its overbreadth constitutes a severe invasion of the right to freedom of expression , 286 and its vagueness only exacerbates that severity.287 The vagueness and severity are compounded by Council 's failure to decide on consequences of breach of the second resolution . Currently , academics do not know what happens if they collaborate contrary to the second resolution -- it may well include disciplinary sanction.288 <p> 136 . The overbreadth does not end there . The principle underlying Council 's second resolution is that Council may prohibit relations with academics of a certain nationality or affiliation if Council considers their affiliated country or entity associated with allegations of possible unlawful conduct . This overbreadth is severe . The second resolution sets a precedent that Council could restrict academic relations with untold numbers of other academics . For instance , it could on this basis restrict relations with academics affiliated with American , Chinese , Iranian , or Russian entities.289 <p> 137 . We have also addressed the deficient link between the second resolution and its purpose . It is not reasonably capable of achieving its purpose , and protecting UCT 's reputation , because it excludes the many ways in which UCT may become associated with allegations of possible unlawful conduct ( even unlawful conduct by only the IDF or Israel ) . <p> 138 . There are many less restrictive means available to the university to protect itself from associations with unlawful conduct . Most obviously , it can sanction or expel UCT members who become associated or complicit in actual unlawful conduct ( after proper and fair inquiry ) . By doing so , it ensures that it ( a ) addresses all potential associations with actual unlawful conduct and ( b ) does not prohibit legitimate academic collaborations . Again , everyone wins . <p> 139 . Additionally , UCT could consider issuing statements distancing itself from any unlawful conduct committed by the IDF , but reiterating , as it did in the March 2019 resolution , that " individual academics , students , and departments are free to engage in academic pursuits with anyone as they wish guided by their own conscience " .290 <p> F. GROUND FIVE : FAILURE TO CONSULT <p> 140 . Council failed to consult with stakeholders and the UCT community before passing the resolutions.291 Council did not consult , for example , with Jewish members of the UCT community , 292 the PSF , the Neuroscience Institute , 293 academics with existing relationships with Israeli academics , 294 and experts on antisemitism and Israel within ( or outside of ) UCT . Council did not consult with donors who expressed concerns about the resolutions.295 <p> 141 . It was irrational to omit the views of these stakeholders in the process leading up to Council 's decision . <p> 141.1 . If the purpose of the first resolution was to adopt a better definition of antisemitism , 296 then excluding the views of Jewish students and faculty in the process leading up to that resolution can not further that purpose.297 As the applicant puts it : " Council decided on antisemitism without the Jews . " 298 This is irrationality par excellence . <p> 141.2 . If Council sought to pass both resolutions in the best interests of the university , then it could not achieve that purpose without considering the views of those members of the community affected by its decision , like the Neuroscience Institute , academics with ties to Israeli academics , and students whose funding may be withdrawn due to the resolutions . For this reason , Council in 2019 decided to hear the views of the UCT community before taking a view on the March 2019 resolution . <p> 142 . Additionally , Council bore a duty to consult stakeholders under the King IV Code , which is incorporated by clause 7.1 of UCT 's Risk Management Policy of June 2020 . The Code obliges Council to adopt a " stakeholder-inclusive approach " when taking key decisions , which includes a consideration of stakeholder interests.299 The Reporting Regulations , moreover , require Council to consult with stakeholders before taking key decisions.300 Council did not adhere to these duties . <p> G. GROUND SIX : A REASONABLE APPREHENSION OF BIAS <p> 143 . A reasonable apprehension of bias arises when a decision-maker is perceived to have associated themselves with one side of a dispute or a certain outcome to a decision . Those exercising public power are entitled to have opinions or predispositions . However , when there is a reasonable apprehension that a decision-maker has prejudged a matter , then their decision is reviewable . Decision-makers can not be seen to approach matters with minds shut to evidence relevant to the matter before them.301 <p> 144 . For instance , if a decision-maker expresses " undisguised hostility mingled , on occasion , with disgust " regarding a matter or party before them , then that gives rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias.302 <p> 145 . In this matter , Council members and UCT have created a reasonable apprehension of bias . We have addressed above why the failure to disclose known risks of losing three donations because of the two resolutions demonstrates bias , or a reasonable apprehension thereof , on the part of the Chair and Exco . But there are five additional reasons for why a reasonable apprehension of bias arises in this case . <p> 146 . First , the Chair and certain Council members considered the DGF , the Dell Foundation , and any donor who may have withdrawn funding due to the resolutions to be hostage takers , 303 " pro-Israel " , 304 and manipulative.305 <p> 146.1 . The Chair and Council members repeatedly allege that donors who might have opposed the resolutions aim to compromise UCT 's values and autonomy.306 <p> 146.2 . At least one Council member considers the DGF trustees to have used " strong arm tactics " 307 and to have " questionable backgrounds , comparing it to potentially accepting funds from organised crime " .308 <p> 146.3 . This same Council member goes on to allege that " recent activities " of these " donors loyal to Israel have been about intentional ideological control through financial coercion " .309 <p> 146.4 . She considers the DGF to be one of these " pro-Israel " donors310 -- who are " uncritical of Israel or its actions " 311 -- seeking to impose conditions on donations that are a " clear violation of academic freedom and institutional autonomy " .312 <p> 147 . These views about donors who may have had concerns with or even opposed the two resolutions create a reasonable apprehension of bias . <p> 147.1 . Council never consulted donors -- whether " pro-Israel " or otherwise -- before taking its decision . But Council members prejudged those donors who may have issues with the two resolutions . Council members decided , without considering donor views or concerns , that these donors sought to " impose on UCT a Zionist worldview , uncritical of Israel or its actions " .313 They have demonstrated a hostility to these donors . <p> 147.2 . Council members accused donors concerned about the two resolutions with improperly advancing a political agenda.314 But there is no similar concern with how some Council members , 315 supportive donors , 316 and indeed the impugned Council resolutions also advance a political agenda . The two resolutions passed by Council are political ; they entail UCT " taking a stand " on a political issue.317 <p> Yet the concern with a " political agenda " tracks only those donors critical of the two resolutions . This contributes to a reasonable apprehension of bias . <p> 148 . Second , Council members have accused those opposing the two resolutions of being part of a " ' zionist ' or ' pro-zionist ' plot " .318 Council members accuse other members of being " Zionists with a political agenda " when members attempt to deal with governance concerns arising from this litigation.319 They bemoan : " we are being held ransom by the Zionists on our council " .320 Council members thus refuse to consider the possibility that the impugned resolutions ought not to have been passed in the way they were passed , expressing " hostility " and resorting to " conspiracy theories " in response to those who question Council 's decision to pass the resolutions.321 This indicates , to a reasonable person , that Council members are biased in favour of the resolutions . <p> 149 . Third , Council members have publicly expressed strong , unqualified views on the issues underpinning the two resolutions . <p> 150 . A Council member describes Israel as " evil " , 322 with a foundation " based on genocide " , 323 and a grave threat to world peace.324 He thinks -- categorically -- that Israel should not exist as a Jewish state.325 He is convinced that antisemitism is weaponised to silence criticism of Israel.326 He has described ( at best for him ) supporters of Israel327 as " a group of messianic lunatics , addicted to killing and destroying " .328 He describes this litigation as a coordinated effort by the " pro-Israel lobby " to suppress criticism of Israel.329 <p> 151 . Another member of Council confirms that at the meeting of 22 June 2024 , this member " was not willing to adopt any position that accommodated the concerns expressed by Council members " .330 This is confirmed by the transcript of the meeting . The transcript reveals that this Council member did not permit nuance.331 <p> 151.1 . This member stressed that Council should either reject or support the resolutions ( there was no possibility of a middle ground , like noting the resolutions or toning them down ) .332 <p> 151.2 . He alleged that the IHRA definition is " simply " being weaponised333 ( despite at least one other Council member querying this simplicity ) .334 <p> 151.3 . He denied that there would be implications for the university ; he asked another Council member whether they are " attempting to create some kind of fear " by asking after implications.335 <p> 151.4 . He dismissed concerns raised by a lawyer on Council as " legal opinion in hyperbole " .336 <p> 151.5 . He implied that those questioning whether Council should pass the resolutions were quibblers akin to bystanders in 1935 Germany or during apartheid.337 He moved for the resolutions , certainly the second resolution , on the ground that Israel is clearly committing a genocide.338 <p> 152 . People are obviously entitled to have opinions . But when exercising public power , functionaries can not allow their views and expression of their views to create a reasonable apprehension that they did not apply an open mind to the decision . These expressions of views , certainly at the meeting of 22 June 2024 , while legitimate in a private capacity , overstep the mark permissible when exercising public power . <p> 153 . Fourth , UCT has issued an official statement in which it describes allegations of antisemitism on campus as " fake news " circulated by " a particular Jewish publication " , which is " alarmist and exaggerated " , and aimed at furthering a political agenda.339 The statement communicates that UCT has prejudged and determined issues concerning the definition of antisemitism , the prevalence of antisemitism , and the abuse of definitions of antisemitism -- issues implicated by the first resolution . <p> 154 . Fifth , taken together with the procedural irregularities leading to its decision , 340 Council 's opposition to this application contributes to a reasonable apprehension of bias.341 This is underlined by the fact that Council persists in its opposition , notwithstanding " serious dissensus within its own ranks " .342 <p> 155 . These five reasons are why an apprehension of bias would appear to a reasonable person who is sensitive to complex social realities . Conversely stated , these five reasons preclude a suggestion that the applicant , in asserting a reasonable apprehension of bias , is hypersensitive , cynical , and suspicious.343 <p> 156 . Accordingly , Council 's decision falls to be reviewed for a reasonable apprehension of bias . <p> H. REMEDY <p> 157 . Once a court finds that the applicant has established a ground of review , it has no discretion : it must declare Council 's decision invalid.344 The two resolutions should then be set aside.345 <p> 158 . @@129847984 <h> Israel in Africa -- a friend with no benefits <p> Israel 's surveillance tools are now part of its economic presence in Africa . Photo : File <p> Last month , Israel opened a new embassy in Lusaka , Zambia , after a 50-year absence . Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar called it part of the " alliance of believers " , adding , " Strengthening our engagement with Africa is a strategic priority . " <p> As the world increasingly unites in criticising the Zionist regime 's occupation and war on Gaza , amplified by the UN declaring it a " genocide of the Palestinian people " , Israel is looking to Africa as a soft power destination . It hopes the pivot to the continent will translate to UN votes and economic benefits . <p> This explains the radical intensification of its diplomatic efforts in Africa , which saw six new Israel Allies Caucuses launched in African parliaments in Ethiopia , C ? te d'Ivoire , Lesotho , Seychelles , Gabon and Guinea-Conakry in July 2025 . In April 2024 , Malawi opened an embassy in Israel and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ September . <p> The caucuses affirm Israel 's right to exist with Jerusalem as its capital and signal the pursuit of expanded cooperation in agriculture , technology , climate resilience and counterterrorism . <p> But how useful is the Israeli partnership to African nations and is Israeli aid nothing more than a debt trap for the struggling nations it claims to assist ? <p> ' Development cooperation ' <p> Israel describes its engagement with Africa as " development cooperation " . Agricultural centres , irrigation projects and training schemes are promoted as gifts of expertise from a small state to a struggling continent . In reality , this is less about solidarity than about power . The financing is structured as buyer 's credits : Israeli banks pay Israeli contractors upfront , export credit agencies insure the risk and African governments guarantee repayment for years to come . If projects fail , the firms are already paid and the banks are protected ; African treasuries -- and citizens -- absorb the loss . <p> This is a classic case of asymmetrical interdependence . Israel cultivates the appearance of soft power @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ structural power , shaping the rules of finance to ensure the benefits flow one way . As former Israeli prime minister Golda Meir admitted after her 1958 Africa tour : " Did we go into Africa because we wanted votes at the United Nations ? Yes , of course ... " <p> What is a buyer 's credit and why is it always in dollars ? <p> Buyer 's credit is when a foreign bank pays an exporter upfront and the importing government promises to repay the bank over time . <p> Step 2 : African government signs a sovereign guarantee to repay over 5 to 10 years . <p> Step 3 : Loan is insured by Israel 's export credit agency Ashra . <p> Repayments are almost always in US dollars or euros -- never local currency -- because export credit agencies insure only in stable currencies . <p> If the local currency depreciates , the debt burden balloons . Governments must use foreign reserves to repay , cutting spending on health , education or subsidies . Citizens pay twice -- once through taxes and again through lost public @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to sever relations with Israel resulting in aid drying up overnight . But , in recent years , Israel has returned with the same formula -- contracts that enrich Israeli firms while locking African citizens into debt service . <p> Ethiopia : Irrigation and debt <p> In 2016 , under then prime minister Hailemariam Desalegn , Ethiopia signed a $200 million buyer 's credit with Israel 's Bank Hapoalim to finance drip irrigation for its sugarcane industry by Netafim . The loan looked like a development partnership , but its structure reveals the imbalance -- Hapoalim paid Netafim directly , Ashra insured the risk and the Ethiopian state carried the liability over 9.5 years at commercial rates . <p> When corruption and mismanagement crippled the sugar sector , the project under-delivered . Netafim had already been paid ; repayments still fell due . Ethiopia spends less than $10 per citizen annually on health and external interest payments absorb around 0.5 to 0.6% of GDP . A single instalment could have vaccinated 2 million children . Instead , scarce resources were diverted to creditors . <p> Zambia : Agro-centres and arrears @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a $47 million buyer 's credit with Israel Discount Bank to fund an " agriculture centre of excellence " contracted to Green-2000 . Insured by Ashra and Dutch export credit agency Atradius , the structure ensured the Israeli contractor was paid upfront while Zambia carried the debt . <p> This came on top of a $176 million Tahal water project announced in 2017 . By the end of 2022 , Zambia 's external arrears reached 15% of GDP , forcing default and restructuring . Hospitals ran short of drugs , teachers went unpaid and rural roads deteriorated as repayments consumed scarce funds . Israeli firms exited whole ; Zambian citizens bore the austerity . <p> Angola : Quiminha and beyond <p> In 2016 -- 17 , under president Jos ? Eduardo dos Santos , Angola awarded Israeli firm Tahal a $370 million contract for the Quiminha agricultural complex , followed by projects worth another $291 million . Financing was opaque but backed by the state . <p> When oil prices crashed , debt service took precedence over social spending , while food insecurity deepened . Israeli contractors profited while Angolans @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ A precedent <p> In the 1960s and 1970s , Israeli loans backed agricultural and mineral projects , including a potash scheme . Many underperformed , but debts endured . Today Uganda still spends about 3.5% of GDP on interest payments , a legacy of reliance on non-concessional loans . <p> Why it matters : Aid framed as " partnership " is risk-free commerce for Israel , debt for Africa . <p> Technology as dependency : Nigeria 's example <p> Israel 's model extends beyond agriculture into technology and security . Nigeria 's embrace of Israeli surveillance tools illustrates how " partnerships " often come with hidden costs and political strings . In 2013 the government contracted Elbit Systems for a $40 million internet monitoring platform and Nigerian law enforcement agencies have since adopted Cellebrite 's phone-extraction tools . <p> Far from constituting aid , these deals lock Nigerian institutions into costly procurement cycles denominated in foreign currency , with little transparency or accountability . Just as agricultural " assistance " has left states paying off irrigation debts , Nigeria 's search for security has tethered it to Israeli surveillance firms @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to overreach and abuse . Israeli technology exports reproduce the same extractive logic as its aid projects : short-term fixes traded for long-term liabilities . <p> Weapons , surveillance and a compromised sovereignty <p> In recent years , Israel 's economic engagement in Africa has aggressively expanded into agritech , cybersecurity and critical infrastructure . By 2014 , market sales of Israeli agricultural technologies ( such as drip irrigation systems ) to African countries had reached $100 million . These sales have continued into 2024 and 2025 . <p> But it is the arms trade that reveals the partnerships ' most disturbing contours . Annual Israeli military exports to African nations embroiled in conflict are estimated between $200 million and $400 million , supplying unmanned aerial vehicles , artillery and surveillance technology to Cameroon , Chad , the Democratic Republic of the Congo , Rwanda and South Sudan . <p> At the end of 2023 Israel Aerospace Industries signed an approximately $1 billion deal over five years to provide Morocco with satellites , particularly the Ofek 13 spy satellites . Additional defence deals with Morocco include $540 million for the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for Heron 1 unmanned aerial vehicles delivered since 2014 . And Israeli company Check Point Software Technologies has established a presence in Casablanca as part of a broader cyber cooperation strategy . <p> Ghana has also engaged in cybersecurity collaboration with Israel , including government-to-government agreements on telecommunications security . <p> This trade is notoriously opaque , yet its consequences are starkly visible . Israeli weapons have been linked to documented war crimes by UN investigators in South Sudan and are wielded by repressive regimes in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea known for torture and extrajudicial killings . Similarly , Israeli spyware and digital surveillance tools have been adopted by governments with weak democratic safeguards , facilitating political repression and mass surveillance . <p> African governments might believe they are purchasing tactical advantages , but they are acquiring entanglement in human rights abuses and political instability . This military and technological cooperation , far from being a neutral exchange , exports the very tools of repression and conflict that undermine African stability and betray the continent 's professed values . <p> The complicity question : arms , debt and African sovereignty @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its moral cost . By eagerly purchasing Israeli arms and spyware , African regimes with poor human rights records , from Cameroon to Chad , are investing not in security but in tools for internal repression , directly undermining the African Union 's Agenda 2063 and UN sustainable development goals . <p> Worse , this relationship creates a profound moral debt trap . This increased trade does not happen in a vacuum , it is intimately tied to Israel 's ongoing genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza . Understanding this sheds vital light on Israel 's true intentions -- racist , colonial and brutal -- - and must serve as a dire warning to African states and civil societies about what the expansion of Israeli power means for African sovereignty and democracy . <p> As Israel faces global condemnation for Gaza , African nations engaging in these deals become tacitly complicit , financing the very war machine destroying Palestinian lives . This is a Faustian bargain -- trading sovereign principles for repression and paying in both drained treasuries and a compromised collective conscience . <p> While some African states deepen @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has leveraged the tools of international law and diplomacy to hold it accountable . Its case of genocide against Israel before the International Court of Justice underscores a fundamental foreign policy choice between pursuing short-term , often repressive , tactical gains and championing a long-term vision for a just international order based on human rights . <p> South Africa has weaponised the law in service of liberation , embodying the anti-colonial solidarity and commitment to human dignity that too many have abandoned . Yet South Africa is not free from Israeli pressure and influence . In August this year , Israel 's minister of digital diplomacy , David Saranga , bypassed diplomatic channels to meet the Amntshangase , amaPondo and abaThembu royal families in the rural Eastern Cape . He offered support from Israel 's Agency for International Development Cooperation , Mashav for local feeding schemes run by traditional authorities , flood disaster relief and extended invitations for them to visit Israel . <p> And despite its International Court of Justice case , South African citizens are having to take to the streets to call on the government to match @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all trade , especially the sale of coal , with Israel , shut the Israeli embassy and arrest South African citizens who have served in theIsrael Defense Forces . <p> African Union and diplomatic fallout <p> Israel 's re-entry has not gone unchallenged . In 2021 the African Union granted Israel observer status . Within two years it was suspended after member states protested , citing solidarity with Palestine . Israeli diplomats were expelled from AU summits in 2023 and 2025 , underscoring the depth of opposition . <p> South Africa has led resistance . In late 2023 , its parliament voted to close the Israeli embassy in Pretoria unless a Gaza ceasefire was reached . Protests outside the embassy continue , framing Israeli aid and technology as part of the same extractive system . <p> Operation Solomon : Humanitarianism or control ? <p> In 1991 , Operation Solomon airlifted more than 14 000 Ethiopian Jews to Israel in 36 hours , projecting rescue and solidarity . Yet , two decades later , reports revealed Ethiopian women in Israel had been given long-acting contraceptives without informed consent . What was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ how " humanitarian " aid masks asymmetrical power . <p> Conclusion <p> From Meir 's frank admission that Africa was about UN votes to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's refrain that , " Israel is coming back to Africa , " the strategy has been consistent . Israeli " aid " and technology exports are not free . They are structured to secure guaranteed profits and political leverage : banks and contractors are paid upfront , export credit agencies remove their risk and African citizens repay the loans or maintain costly imports . <p> Ethiopia 's sugar projects , Zambia 's agro-centres , Angola 's Quiminha complex , Nigeria 's surveillance contracts and Watergen machines from South Africa to Sierra Leone all point to the same conclusion -- development promised , dependency delivered . <p> For Israel , Africa provides contracts , votes and legitimacy . For African citizens , it too often means austerity , debt service and surveillance . The mask of aid conceals an extractive logic . Israel 's " return to Africa " looks less like partnership -- and more like a system of control . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with over 20 years of experience covering the Horn of Africa , identity politics in Turkiye and Zionism in Africa . @@129861063 <h> POLITICS <h> EFF rejects Trump 's 20-point ceasefire plan for Gaza <p> Fighters say this plan is a blueprint for the foreign takeover of Gaza and the erasure of Palestinian sovereignity <p> EFF statement on Trump 's 20-point ceasefire plan for Gaza <p> 30 September 2025 <p> The Economic Freedom Fighters ( EFF ) firmly rejects the so-called 20-point ceasefire plan announced by U.S. President Donald Trump as a solution to Israel 's genocidal war on Gaza . Far from bringing peace , this plan is a blueprint for the foreign takeover of Gaza and the erasure of Palestinian sovereignty . It treats Palestinians not as a people with the right to self-determination , but as passive subjects to be managed , supervised , and rebuilt under the dictates of foreign powers . <p> It has already been established by the international community that what is taking place in Gaza is genocide . The International Court of Justice has explicitly called for Israel to retreat and to cease its murderous campaign against the Palestinian people , while the Intemational Criminal Court has issued warrants of arrest for Benjamin Netanyahu @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ number of countries across the world are recognising Palestine as a sovereign state , affirming the legitimacy of its people 's struggle for freedom and dignity . Trump 's plan must , therefore , be understood as a desperate attempt to divert attention from these global shifts , to normalise occupation , and to repackage domination under the guise of " peace . " <p> The proposal to establish a " Board of Peace " chaired by Trump himself and including Tony Blair is an insult to the Palestinian struggle and to all victims of imperialist wars . Tony Blair , a war criminal who played a leading role in the illegal invasion of Iraq and the deaths of hundreds of thousands , can not possibly be trusted with guiding peace or reconstruction . <p> His presence exposes the true intent of the plan as not to end violence , but to entrench the same imperialist forces that have destabilised the Middle East for decades . <p> --&gt; <p> The scheme to install this technocratic committee in Ga7a , backed by an Intemational Stabilisation Force trained by the United States @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ than occupation by another name . Trump 's plan openly places Gaza under external control , with Israel retaining the power to dictate timelines , security perimeters , and the conditions under which territory may be " handed over . " Furthermore , the Palestinian Authority is expected to undergo " reforms " before it can be trusted to govern . <p> In other words , Palestinians are told that they can not rule themselves until they meet conditions imposed by foreign powers , which is nothing more than a colonial arrangement . <p> Equally alarming is the demand for the total dismantling of Gaza 's armed resistance infrastructure without any redress for the underlying causes of resistance : occupation , dispossession , blockade , and statelessness . By criminalising Palestinian resistance while leaving Israel 's military supremacy unchallenged , the plan strips Palestinians of their right to defend themselves and ensures their permanent subjugation . <p> Another element of the plan is the economic framing which includes talk of special economic zones , reduced tariffs , redevelopment driven by foreign investment , and massive reconstruction funding . However , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , who benefits , and what guarantees exist that Palestinians themselves will have decision-making power , access , and that wealth will not be extracted rather than shared . <p> --&gt; <p> There is no solid plan clarifying land restitution , or how the vast damage to homes , infrastructure , health and education systems will be repaired from below , in partnership with local communities . With no acknowledgment of occupied territory , no clear mechanism to stop expansion of settlements , no pathway to justice for war crimes , and no entrenchment of Palestinians ' rights under international law , mechanism for submission rather than peace . <p> In sum , this plan offers many superficial promises such as hostage release , aid flow , and reconstruction but when scrutinised in full context it is deeply imbalanced . It hands over control over Gaza 's political , security , economic , and social life to external oversight , while denying Palestinians the full rights and agency that must be the foundation of any just peace . It is simply designed to manage Gaza under new architecture , while @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> As a result , the EFF denounces this plan as a neocolonial project designed to pacify the oppressed while securing the interests of imperial powers and their allies in Israel . It offers no solid plan for the future of Gaza , nor any genuine path to an end of occupation . True peace will never come from schemes drafted in Washington or London . It will only come when the people of Palestine , in Gaza and beyond , are free to determine their own future , reclaim their land , and live with dignity and justice . <p> We call on all progressive forces across the world , particularly in Africa and the Global South , to reject Trump 's 20-point plan with the contempt it deserves . We stand firmly with the people of Palestine , and we will continue to support their just struggle for freedom , sovereignty , and the right of return . <p> --&gt; <p> Issued by Sinawo Thambo , National Spokesperson , EFF , 30 September 2025
